links.outcome: AO/OTA 31A vs 31B classification accuracy with RAG grounding versus zero-shot and few-shot prompting
links.effect: RAG accuracy 94.29% (F1 94.29%) equaled zero-shot 94.29% (F1 94.28%); few-shot dropped to 88.57% (F1 88.53%). RAG showed no measurable advantage in binary classification.
links.quote: Zero‑shot prompting attained the same accuracy (94.29%, F1 = 94.28%), while few‑shot learning unexpectedly dropped to 88.57% (F1 = 88.53%).

links.outcome: Accuracy of initial 31C labels on expert re-adjudication
links.effect: Of 47 cases initially labeled 31C, only 6 (12.8%) met true AO/OTA 31C criteria; 41 (87.2%) were acetabular fractures or misclassified 31A/31B cases.
links.quote: A key finding was that after expert re‑adjudication of 47 cases initially labeled as 31C, only 6 (12.8%) met the true AO/OTA 31C criteria; the remaining 41 (87.2%) were actually acetabular fractures (AO/OTA type 61) or misclassified 31A/31B cases.
